1.title: Jökulsárlón & Diamond Beach in a Day

periods.title: Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon
periods.text: Arrive early at Jökulsárlón glacier lagoon, the deepest lake in Iceland at 248 metres, filled with icebergs calved from Breiðamerkurjökull glacier. Walk the western shore trail for the best angles of ice chunks ranging from brilliant white to deep blue streaked with volcanic ash. Seals haul out on the ice and swim between the bergs. The scale is humbling: some icebergs are the size of houses.
periods.tip: Arrive before 9am for soft morning light and fewer tour buses. The lagoon faces south, so morning sun hits the glacier wall beautifully.

periods.title: Boat Tour Among the Icebergs
periods.text: Take a zodiac boat tour (11,000 ISK, 1 hour) to weave between the icebergs and approach the glacier wall. Guides break off chunks of 1,000-year-old ice for you to hold. The amphibian boat tour (6,500 ISK, 40 minutes) is a cheaper alternative but doesn't get as close. Afterward, walk across the road to Diamond Beach: clear glacier ice chunks wash ashore on jet-black volcanic sand, glittering in the light.
periods.tip: The zodiac tour is worth the premium: you get within metres of towering icebergs and the glacier face. Book the first afternoon slot.

periods.title: Diamond Beach Sunset & Höfn
periods.text: Spend sunset at Diamond Beach watching waves tumble ice fragments onto the black sand: each piece catches the golden light differently. The beach changes hourly as tides deposit new ice. Drive 80 minutes east to Höfn for the night, the langoustine capital of Iceland. Dinner at Pakkhús (langoustine tails from 4,900 ISK) or the Höfn Noodle Station for warming lamb soup (1,790 ISK).
periods.tip: Diamond Beach ice is constantly shifting: visit at different tides for completely different compositions. Low tide exposes more ice.

periods.title: Svartifoss Waterfall Hike
periods.text: Start at the Skaftafell Visitor Centre in Vatnajökull National Park. Hike to Svartifoss (Black Falls), a striking waterfall framed by dark hexagonal basalt columns that inspired the design of Hallgrímskirkja church. The 5.5km round trip trail gains 120 metres of elevation through birch woodland, taking about 90 minutes. Continue to the Sjónarnípa viewpoint for dramatic views across the vast glacial outwash plain.
periods.tip: Start by 8:30am to beat the tour bus crowds. The basalt columns at Svartifoss are most dramatic when wet: light rain is your friend.

periods.title: Skaftafellsjökull Glacier Hike
periods.text: Join a guided glacier walk on Skaftafellsjökull or Falljökull (12,990 ISK, 3–4 hours). Crampons and ice axes are provided as you trek across blue ice, crevasses, moulins, and ridges of volcanic ash. No experience necessary: guides teach you to walk confidently on ice. The glacier's surface is a frozen landscape of sculptures carved by meltwater, constantly shifting and cracking around you.
periods.tip: Wear sturdy ankle-supporting hiking boots: crampons attach to your own boots. Bring sunglasses as the ice glare is intense.

periods.title: Campsite & Glacier Views
periods.text: Set up camp at Skaftafell campsite (1,800 ISK per person), one of Iceland's best-equipped sites with showers, cooking shelters, and stunning views of Öræfajökull, Iceland's highest peak. Take the evening trail to the Skaftafellsheiði viewpoint for golden-hour views of multiple glacier tongues descending from the ice cap. Cook dinner at camp using supplies from Höfn or Vík.
periods.tip: The campsite fills fast in summer: arrive before 4pm to secure a spot. Alternatively, book Hótel Skaftafell 5 minutes away.

periods.title: Jökulsárlón Glacier Lagoon
periods.text: Drive 45 minutes east to Jökulsárlón. Walk the shoreline trails on both sides of the lagoon: the western bank gives the widest panorama while the eastern side gets you closer to where icebergs enter the lagoon. The bergs range from pristine white to deep blue, some with dramatic black ash stripes from volcanic eruptions trapped in the ice over centuries. Seals bob between the ice.
periods.tip: Bring binoculars for seal-spotting on the far ice floes. A telephoto lens or 10x phone zoom captures them resting beautifully.

periods.title: Zodiac Boat Tour & Fjallsárlón
periods.text: Take the zodiac boat tour (11,000 ISK) for an intimate journey between the icebergs. Guides crack off ancient ice so you can taste thousand-year-old glacier water. Then drive 10 minutes west to Fjallsárlón, a smaller, less-visited glacier lagoon with an equally dramatic glacier wall but far fewer tourists. The zodiac tour here (9,900 ISK) gets even closer to the calving ice face.
periods.tip: Fjallsárlón is Jökulsárlón's quieter twin. On busy summer days, skip the crowds and come here first for a more intimate experience.

periods.title: Diamond Beach at Golden Hour
periods.text: Cross Route 1 to Diamond Beach and spend the evening watching ice wash ashore. Each wave deposits new crystal-clear chunks that melt gradually over hours, creating an ever-changing gallery. The low-angle evening sun turns the ice into prisms of colour. This is one of the most photogenic spots in Iceland: bring a tripod for long-exposure shots of waves swirling around the glowing ice.
periods.tip: Get low to the ground for dramatic shots: placing your camera at ice level with the sunset behind creates stunning backlit compositions.

periods.title: Natural Ice Cave Tour
periods.text: In winter (November–March), join an ice cave tour inside Vatnajökull glacier (19,990 ISK, 3–4 hours from Jökulsárlón). Walk inside cathedral-sized chambers of luminous blue ice: the colour intensifies with thicker ice and changes with the weather. In summer, substitute with a glacier hike on Breiðamerkurjökull or a kayaking tour on the lagoon (14,990 ISK) for a water-level perspective among the bergs.
periods.tip: Ice caves are only accessible November–March when temperatures are cold enough. Book early: these tours sell out months ahead.

periods.title: Vestrahorn & Stokksnes
periods.text: Drive 80 minutes east to Stokksnes peninsula (900 ISK entry at the Viking Café). Vestrahorn mountain rises 454 metres in dramatic jagged peaks above a black sand dune landscape. At low tide, the wet sand creates mirror reflections of the mountain, one of Iceland's most iconic photography locations. Explore the abandoned Viking film set on the beach and walk the dunes beneath the towering peaks.
periods.tip: Check tide tables: Vestrahorn reflections only work at low tide when water sits on the flat sand. Overcast days create moody drama.

periods.title: Höfn & Langoustine Feast
periods.text: End in Höfn, a small fishing town famous for langoustine (Icelandic lobster). Dinner at Pakkhús in the old harbour warehouse (langoustine feast from 6,900 ISK) or Humarhöfnin for the classic langoustine soup (2,990 ISK). Walk along the harbour at sunset with views of Vatnajökull glacier dominating the skyline. The annual Humarhátíð (Lobster Festival) in late June is worth timing your visit for.
periods.tip: Pakkhús and Humarhöfnin both need reservations in summer. Book ahead or arrive right when they open at 6pm.

budgetTips.title: Self-cater at campsites
budgetTips.text: Iceland's restaurants average 3,000–5,500 ISK per meal. Shop at Bónus or Krónan supermarkets and cook at campsite kitchens. A Camping Card (19,900 ISK) covers 28 nights across Iceland.

budgetTips.title: Free natural attractions
budgetTips.text: Jökulsárlón, Diamond Beach, all waterfalls, canyons, and black sand beaches are free. The most spectacular sights in southeast Iceland cost nothing: spend your budget on experiences instead.

budgetTips.title: Share a rental car
budgetTips.text: A rental car split between 3–4 people is cheaper than tours. Economy cars start at 8,000 ISK/day. Use the Samferda.net rideshare site to find travel companions for fuel splitting.

budgetTips.title: Skip the Blue Lagoon
budgetTips.text: At 7,990+ ISK, it's Iceland's priciest swim. The Secret Lagoon (3,000 ISK) and local pools like Vesturbæjarlaug (1,150 ISK) are cheaper and more authentic Icelandic experiences.

budgetTips.title: Bring a refillable bottle
budgetTips.text: Icelandic tap water is pure glacial water: never buy bottled. Fill up at any tap, campsite, or stream away from agricultural land. It's the best water you'll ever taste.

budgetTips.title: Book activities online ahead
budgetTips.text: Glacier hikes, zodiac tours, and ice caves are cheaper when booked online in advance. Walk-up prices are 10–20% higher and popular tours sell out, especially in July and August.

budgetBreakdown.notes: Fuel share → rental car → guided tours with transport
Free sights → zodiac tour → ice cave + glacier hike
Supermarket beer → pub pints → cocktails in Höfn

practicalInfo.title: Visa & Entry
items: Iceland is in the Schengen Area. EU/EEA citizens need only an ID card. US, Canadian, Australian citizens get 90 days visa-free
Fly into Keflavík Airport (KEF). Jökulsárlón is 380km east of Reykjavík, a 4.5-hour drive along Route 1
Domestic flights to Höfn from Reykjavík Airport (15 minutes) are available but expensive. Driving is the standard approach

practicalInfo.title: Getting Around
items: A rental car is essential: there is no public transport to Jökulsárlón. 2WD is fine on Route 1 year-round if conditions are clear
In winter (October–April), a 4WD is strongly recommended. Roads can be icy and snow-covered. Check road.is for conditions daily
The drive from Reykjavík to Jökulsárlón is 380km, taking 4.5–5 hours. Most visitors break the journey with south coast stops

practicalInfo.title: Connectivity
items: Mobile signal is reliable along Route 1 but drops between towns. Download offline maps before leaving Reykjavík
Síminn and Vodafone tourist SIMs (2,000 ISK) at Keflavík Airport provide 5–10GB data with coverage along the south coast
WiFi is available at hotels and guesthouses. Campsites usually have WiFi at the reception building only

practicalInfo.title: Money
items: Cards accepted everywhere in Iceland, even rural activity operators and campsites. You rarely need cash
ATMs in Vík and Höfn but not at Jökulsárlón itself. Ensure your card works internationally before the trip
No tipping culture in Iceland. All prices include service. Tip only for exceptional guided experiences if desired

practicalInfo.title: Weather & Packing
items: Southeast Iceland is one of the wettest regions. Summer: 8–14°C with frequent rain. Winter: -5–3°C with wind and snow
Pack: waterproof jacket and trousers, warm fleece, thermals, waterproof hiking boots, hat, gloves, and sunglasses for glacier glare
Check vedur.is daily for weather and safetravel.is for safety alerts. Conditions change rapidly and glacial wind is brutal

practicalInfo.title: Health & Safety
items: The nearest hospital is in Höfn (small) or Selfoss (larger). Carry a well-stocked first aid kit in your rental car
Register your travel plan at safetravel.is. Mountain rescue is free but they prefer prevention: always tell someone your plans
Emergency: 112. Iceland has excellent helicopter rescue but response time to the southeast can be 1–2 hours in bad weather

culturalTips.title: Glacier Safety
culturalTips.text: Never walk on a glacier without a certified guide and proper equipment. Crevasses are hidden and deadly. All glacier tours in Iceland use qualified guides with rescue training.

culturalTips.title: Leave No Trace
culturalTips.text: Iceland's landscape is extraordinarily fragile. Never step on moss (it takes decades to regrow), don't stack rocks, don't fly drones without permits, and pack out all rubbish.

culturalTips.title: Wildlife Distance
culturalTips.text: Keep 20 metres from seals, avoid disturbing nesting birds, and never chase or feed wildlife. Puffins, Arctic terns, and seals are protected: observe quietly from a respectful distance.

culturalTips.title: Driving Etiquette
culturalTips.text: Pull fully off the road to take photos: Icelandic roads are narrow and stopping on the highway is dangerous and illegal. Use designated pullouts and car parks only.

culturalTips.title: Pool Culture
culturalTips.text: Shower naked without a swimsuit before entering any Icelandic pool: signs explain the procedure and it's strictly enforced. This is a deeply ingrained cultural norm, not a tourist oddity.

culturalTips.title: Ocean Respect
culturalTips.text: Icelandic waves are powerful and unpredictable. Sneaker waves at Reynisfjara and Diamond Beach have killed tourists. Never turn your back on the sea and maintain safe distance.
